title: Learning complex temporal dependencies via local synaptic plasticity
authors: Ng-Kee-Kwong, J.; Tang, M.; Akam, T.; Bogacz, R.
abstract: The ability to extract and exploit temporal structure across diverse tasks is central to human cognition. Neuroscientists have typically relied on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT) when modelling neural and behavioural processes such as decision-making and motor control. However, this algorithm has limited biological plausibility, hence the computational principles underlying efficient learning of temporal dependencies remain unresolved. Here, we investigate temporal predictive coding (tPC), a recently proposed framework that extends predictive coding to the temporal domain while preserving local Hebbian update rules. We analyse and extend tPC to establish its relationship with several influential computational models of learning in RNNs, including BPTT, reservoir computing, and eligibility propagation (e-prop). We first demonstrate structurally equivalent weight update rules between tPC and tBPTT1, a variant of BPTT in which gradients are propagated only one time step into the past. We then show that tPC can leverage reservoir dynamics to encode short-range temporal context, and simultaneously sculpt neural trajectories in state space to support downstream readout. We further demonstrate that hierarchical recurrent dynamics can facilitate learning of more complex temporal dependencies, while additionally conferring robustness to strong distractors. Finally, we show that tPC networks can be augmented with biologically inspired eligibility traces to solve temporally extended context-dependent tasks. Together, these results reveal that relatively simple recurrent networks governed by local plasticity can support temporal learning in more complex settings than previously appreciated.

title: IER3-N-cadherin axis contributes to apoptosis resistance in dermal fibroblasts under profibrotic conditions
authors: Ichimura, R.; Nakajima, H.; Sugimori, A.; Sumida, H.
abstract: Background: Persistent activation and resistance to apoptosis of dermal fibroblasts contribute to pathological skin fibrosis. Immediate early response 3 (IER3) is a stress-responsive protein involved in cell survival, but its role in cutaneous fibrosis remains unclear. We investigated the functional significance of IER3 in dermal fibroblasts and its potential contribution to fibrosis. Methods: IER3 expression was examined in skin samples from patients with systemic sclerosis, keloids, and hypertrophic scars. Primary human dermal fibroblasts were stimulated with transforming growth factor-{beta}1 (TGF-{beta}1). RNA sequencing, siRNA-mediated gene silencing, quantitative PCR, and flow cytometric apoptosis assays were performed to investigate the downstream mechanisms and functional consequences of IER3 expression. Results: IER3 expression was increased in dermal fibroblasts within fibrotic skin lesions and was induced by TGF-{beta}1 independently of SMAD3 and MEK/ERK signaling. Transcriptomic analysis identified CDH2, encoding N-cadherin, as a downstream target of IER3. Moreover, TGF-{beta}1 induced CDH2 expression in a SMAD3 phosphorylation-dependent manner. IER3 knockdown attenuated TGF-{beta}1-induced CDH2 expression, whereas CDH2 knockdown did not affect IER3 expression. Furthermore, CDH2 knockdown enhanced staurosporine-induced apoptosis in TGF-{beta}1-stimulated fibroblasts, accompanied by a shift in apoptosis-related gene expression toward a pro-apoptotic profile. Conclusion: Our findings identify a previously unrecognized IER3-N-cadherin regulatory axis that may promote dermal fibroblast survival by suppressing apoptosis under profibrotic conditions. Targeting this pathway may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for persistent skin fibrosis.

title: Lac1-dependent ceramide synthesis couples septum assembly to cell separation in Schizosaccharomyces pombe
authors: Serrano Caravaca, A. M.; Gomez Delgado, L.; Hanaoka, K.; Matsunaga, K.; Funato, K.; Garcia Cortes, J. C.; Ribas, J. C.; Alcaide Gavilan, M.; Flor Parra, I.; Lucena Hernandez, R.
abstract: Ceramides are precursors of complex sphingolipids and bioactive membrane lipids. In the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, they are produced by a ceramide synthase with two catalytic subunits, Lac1 and Lag1, which are redundant but not functionally equivalent: only Lac1 is required for normal growth and cell size. Why Lac1 has this unique role, and how ceramide synthesis contributes to cell morphogenesis, remain unknown. Here, we show that Lac1 couples septum assembly to cell separation. Cells lacking Lac1 die predominantly during cell separation and build septa with a thinner primary layer and markedly thicker secondary layers, accompanied by altered deposition of {beta}-(1,3)-glucans and galactomannan. These defects are not rescued by osmotic stabilization. The essential glucan synthase Bgs4 is mislocalized to cytoplasmic granules, and total {beta}-(1,3)-glucan synthase activity is partially reduced. Nevertheless, Ags1, Bgs1 and Bgs4 accumulate to higher levels and persist almost twice as long at the division site, indicating defective clearance rather than delivery of the septum-synthesis machinery. Plasma membrane sterol distribution remains unaffected. To accurately impair ceramide synthesis, we isolated thermosensitive lac1-ts alleles in a lag1{Delta} background. Their substitutions cluster in the conserved TRAM/LAG1 domain. Metabolic labeling showed that these alleles reduce ceramide synthesis at the restrictive temperature. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that two substitutions perturb distinct contacts with C26-CoA, while Lac1-M167T loses its endoplasmic reticulum localization. Acute inactivation recapitulates the deletion phenotype, causing septum accumulation and cell death. Together, our findings establish that Lac1-dependent ceramide synthesis is required for the orderly completion of septum assembly and cell separation.

title: Human senataxin uses distinct peripheral elements to unwind R-loops and act on RNA polymerase II
authors: Lanicek, M.; Sedova, K.; Hasanova, Z.; Porrua, O.; Sebesta, M.
abstract: Persistent R-loops and paused or stalled RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) elongation complexes can threaten genome stability. Senataxin (SETX) contributes to R-loop resolution and RNAPII regulation, but their intimate connection during transcription makes the individual contributions of these activities difficult to distinguish in cells. To determine whether these activities rely on the same molecular features, we investigated the structure and biochemical properties of the SETX helicase domain (SETX-HD). Cryo-EM defines the conserved helicase core and RNA-binding channel of SETX-HD, while biochemical analyses identify distinct roles for two peripheral elements: a previously uncharacterised C-terminal RNA-binding domain (CT-RBD) and the prong subdomain. In reconstituted mammalian transcription assays, SETX-HD promotes passage beyond a defined RNAPII pause and elongation-complex dissociation on the same template. The CT-RBD stabilises RNA engagement and is required for efficient R-loop unwinding, whereas its deletion preserves both RNAPII-associated activities. Conversely, replacing the native SETX prong with its fungal Sen1 counterpart preserves R-loop unwinding but impairs both RNAPII outcomes. These reciprocal separation-of-function effects establish that a common SETX-HD RNA-translocation core depends on distinct peripheral elements for R-loop unwinding and action on mammalian RNAPII. This separation provides a direct route to determine how these activities contribute to SETX function in cells.

title: A compact motif vocabulary is differentially interpreted across human cell types
abstract: How a common genome generates diverse human cell types may depend less on distinct cis-regulatory vocabularies than on context-dependent use of a shared one. We have developed CNN-CR, an interpretable neural network that learns regulatory motifs while predicting gene expression across 116 human biosamples. Promoter regulation proves highly compressible: dozens of recurrent motif families retain most of the predictive information of much larger cell-type-specific vocabularies and generalize to cellular contexts excluded from their discovery. These motifs are conserved at their binding sites and enriched at fine-mapped regulatory variants. Cellular context acts at two levels: chromatin state gates which motif instances are available for regulatory use, whereas reader identity determines how accessible motifs are interpreted. ChIP-seq data reveal frequent shifts in reader occupancy across cell types, and genome-scale perturbations support corresponding context-dependent reader functions. Thus, regulatory diversity can emerge through differential access to and interpretation of a compact shared DNA vocabulary.

title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Protein Language Models for Dual-Target Antimicrobial Peptide Discovery Under Strict Homology Constraints
abstract: The worldwide escalation of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a severe challenge to modern public health, necessitating novel classes of therapeutic agents. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) represent highly promising alternatives to small-molecule antibiotics due to their co-evolutionary resilience and rapid membrane disruption dynamics. However, translating computational AMP leads into clinical drug candidates remains bottlenecked by off-target cytotoxicity, predominantly hemolytic activity against mammalian erythrocytes. Although pretrained foundational protein language models (PLMs) have rapidly advanced molecular property prediction, current architectures frequently isolate antibacterial potency and cytotoxicity into disconnected single-task pipelines or succumb to catastrophic performance drops under strict homology-controlled evaluations. Recently, the Quantitative Mapping of Antimicrobial Peptides (QMAP) benchmark proposed that frozen PLM embeddings show weak linearly accessible features for hemolytic activity (HC50) resulting in poor rank correlation ({rho} < 0.25) on out-of-distribution sequence splits. In this work, we introduce an end-to-end multi-task parameter-efficient transfer learning framework designed to simultaneously optimize antibacterial potency and minimize mammalian cytotoxicity without sequence leakage. Built upon ESM-2 (150M), our architecture incorporates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) into self-attention projections, fine-tuning approx 0.70% of model weights. To restore gradient interference originating from disparate membrane lysis mechanisms, we implement an adaptive multi-task loss guided by Kendall homoscedastic uncertainty weighting. Evaluated across predefined QMAP benchmark splits enforcing a 60% maximal sequence identity threshold, our joint architecture remarkably outperforms conventional linear probes, tree-based regressors, and frozen foundational models. The framework achieves an E. coli potency rank correlation of {rho} = 0.6132 (r = 0.6816) and successfully elevates hemolytic toxicity correlation to {rho} = 0.5374 (r = 0.5541). To establish real world utility, we deploy the optimized joint network to screen a curated in silico library of 749 de-novo designed peptides, successfully isolating selective cationic-amphipathic candidates possessing Therapeutic Indices (TI = HC50/MIC) up to 144.03 while effectively deprioritizing broadly lytic motifs (TI < 2.0). These findings demonstrate that parameter-efficient adaptation unlocks fine-grained bioactive structural semantics in foundational PLMs, providing an accurate, scalable framework for therapeutic peptide engineering.

title: Redesigning the Eterna100 RNA design benchmark for the Vienna 2 folding engine
authors: Koodli, R. V.; Rudolfs, B.; Romano, J.; Wayment-Steele, H. K.; Dunlap, W. A.; Eterna Structure Designers,  ; Das, R.
abstract: The rational design of RNA is becoming important for rapidly developing technologies in medicine and biochemistry, spurring development of numerous RNA secondary structure design algorithms and benchmarks to evaluate their performance. However, the problem of RNA design is dependent upon the inverse problem of RNA structure prediction through "folding engines" that predict structure from sequence. We hypothesized that differences in RNA folding engines could impact design algorithms, and recruited an online community of RNA design experts to modify the widely used RNA secondary structure design benchmark Eterna100 to address target unsolvability when changing the folding engine used (ViennaRNA 1 updated to 2). We tested this new Eterna100-V2 benchmark with six RNA design algorithms, and found that the performance of RNA design algorithms changed depending on which folding engine was used in training or evaluation. We further explored algorithms reported to have solved the original Eterna100 and found that incorrect folding engine settings were used in their prior evaluation. As a result, currently, both the original Eterna100-V1 and the modernized Eterna100-V2 benchmark remain unsolved with their intended folding engine settings. This work demonstrates that the design difficulty of RNA structures is intrinsically linked to thermodynamic models and suggests that future RNA design algorithms that can adapt to updated thermodynamic models may result in improved performance. Eterna100-V1 and Eterna100-V2 benchmarks and example solutions are freely available at https://github.com/eternagame/eterna100-benchmarking.

title: Reduced enteric Bdnf expression and TrkB-dependent regulation of Vip in a Mecp2-null mouse model of Rett syndrome-associated gastrointestinal dysmotility
authors: Puttapaka, S. N.; Admasu, I. A.; Scott, A.; Sonmez, G.; Seika, P.; Rajkumar, M.; Valencia, X.; Consorti, A.; Hong, S. M.; Slosberg, J.; Fagiolini, M.; Kulkarni, S.
abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) dysmotility is a highly prevalent and clinically significant feature of Rett syndrome (RTT), yet its underlying mechanisms remain poorly defined. Here, we investigated these mechanisms of GI dysmotility in a Mecp2null mouse model of RTT. First, we observed that MeCP2 was expressed in murine myenteric ganglia, including in enteric neurons and that Mecp2null males developed maturation associated functional regression in their GI motility. In dysmotile mice, longitudinal muscle myenteric plexus tissue showed marked reductions in enteric Bdnf isoforms IV, VI, and II, whereas expression of the BDNF receptor isoforms TrkB.FL and TrkB.T1 was not significantly altered, consistent with reduced enteric BDNF TrkB signaling. Despite impaired GI motility, Mecp2null mice showed no significant changes in total enteric neuronal density, nitrergic neuronal abundance, or expression of Nos1, Chat, and Uchl1. In contrast, Vip expression was significantly reduced, while expression of VIP receptor genes: Vipr1 and Vipr2 was increased, indicating disrupted VIPergic signaling. Integration with publicly available enteric single-cell/nucleus datasets and targeted qRTPCR further suggested altered inhibitory neuronal subtype composition, with reduced Vip+ Cartpt+ signatures and increased Nfia expression, suggesting that MeCP2 loss differentially affects distinct inhibitory neuronal subpopulations. Finally, conditional loss of TrkB.FL in neural crest-derived cells reduced Vip expression without recapitulating the full Mecp2null VIPergic phenotype, indicating that impaired BDNF TrkB signaling contributes to, but does not completely explain, the GI dysmotility in this model of RTT. Together, these findings identify enteric BDNF TrkB and VIPergic dysfunction as key mechanisms underlying GI dysmotility in RTT.

title: Myelin Governs Hippocampal Network Function through the Extracellular Space it Occupies, Not Only the Axons it Insulates
authors: Jia, X.; Zeng, C.; Liu, L.; Gao, T.; Bi, J.; Zeng, Z.; Liang, L.; Qi, C.; Lin, F.; Cheng, F.
abstract: Myelin, the multilamellar sheath wrapping neuronal axons, enables saltatory conduction. Beyond electrical insulation, myelin occupies volume, and therefore shapes the extracellular space (ECS) through which interstitial fluid flows and neurotransmitter diffuses. How these two roles interact is unknown. We built a multi-scale model of hippocampal CA1 coupling lattice Boltzmann simulations of ECS flow to detailed networks of reconstructed neurons and glia. Demyelination enlarged the ECS volume fraction from 28 to 43 per cent up to 43 to 70 per cent across layers, lowered tortuosity from about 1.7 to 1.4, raised effective diffusivity from 0.35 to 0.50 of free solution and shortened solute breakthrough times by roughly a third, while raising flow speed yet lowering viscous dissipation. Because transmitter concentration scales inversely with that volume, synaptic driving force fell: postsynaptic potential amplitude declined with wrap count and transmission failed entirely below four of sixteen wraps. In 200-cell networks, demyelination halved firing (pyramidal 7.9 to 4.4 Hz), rendered discharge burst-dominated, reduced band power by up to 8.7-fold and displaced the population state, which a classifier separated at 100 per cent accuracy, whereas an inflammatory glial census left every functional measure unchanged. Driving myelin continuously from intact to 12.5 per cent and back recovered the same threshold near four wraps, and firing rate and spectral power returned fully to baseline. Myelin thus governs circuit function through the space it vacates as well as the axons it insulates, with opposite consequences for clearance and for signalling, a dissociation that may matter in demyelinating disease.

title: Path knockout: an analysis tool for connectome-driven circuit discovery
abstract: Neural circuits in the brain transform sensory information into perceptual, emotional and motor output. The connectome -- a synaptic-resolution wiring diagram of all neurons in a nervous system -- provides a neuroanatomical blueprint for identifying different circuits that mediate specific computations. However, its sheer scale and complexity pose a significant challenge in extracting functionally relevant multi-synaptic pathways. Here we established path knockout, a connectome analysis method that identifies dominant multi-synaptic pathways. Path knockout uses the input fraction of each synaptic connection as a surrogate for the probability that information transfer succeeds across that synapse and calculates approximate probability, or connection strength, that at least one path succeeds among all multi-synaptic paths between defined source and sink neuron populations. It then quantifies the importance of each interneuron by assessing the impact of its removal on the connection strength. We demonstrate that path knockout outperforms other methods for pathway analysis and identifies known and novel interneurons in the Drosophila circuits. Using path knockout, we identified a convergent circuit motif linking sexually dimorphic aggression command neurons to a shared isomorphic visual pursuit pathway. Path knockout is implemented such that it runs in minutes on a standard computer. Thus, path knockout provides a scalable and generalizable framework for connectome-driven circuit discovery.

title: A medial entorhinal connectome reveals compartmentalized microcircuit architecture
authors: Shi, T.; Chen, Y.; Jin, H.; Jiang, H.; Chen, X.; Xiong, Z.; Wu, F.; Zhang, R.
abstract: The medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) transforms multimodal inputs into spatial representations, but the synaptic architecture underlying its computations remains unclear. Here we generated a synapse-resolution connectomic dataset spanning all six layers of mouse MEC and the adjacent parasubiculum with serial electron microscopy, providing a continuous volume for mapping cellular organization and connectivity across layers and regions. We found that clustered pyramidal neurons in MEC layer II extended oblique apical dendrites with a dorsolateral bias and long-range myelinated axons within the layer. Exhaustive reconstruction of one cluster revealed a central exclusion core (ExC) that spatially partitioned basal dendritic architecture and synaptic connectivity. A spatially constrained growth model reproduced the position-dependent dendritic patterns. Within the ExC, pyramidal neurons formed a compact recurrent excitatory network and converged onto shared inhibitory partners. Basket cells (BC) and recurrent Martinotti cells provided perisomatic and apical-dendritic feedback, respectively. Dense, compact reciprocal connectivity between L2P neurons and BCs within the ExC, together with BC axonal bands extending beyond the ExC, suggests a potential circuit mechanism for generating temporally structured inhibitory output from the pyramidal-cell cluster along directionally extended axons. Together, these findings link cellular-scale geometry and synaptic wiring to emergent circuit dynamics that extend from dense computation within individual clusters to region-wide modulation, providing a connectomic foundation for understanding the circuit basis of spatial navigation.

title: Wolffia globosa -derived nanovesicles as a natural source of bioactive metabolites with neuroprotective potential against methylglyoxal-induced oxidative stress
authors: Khongkla, E.; Boonsnongcheep, P.; Srisaisup, M.; Charuraksa, T.
abstract: Plant-derived nanovesicles (PDNVs) have attracted increasing attention for their potential biomedical applications, particularly in oxidative stress-related diseases and neuroprotection. Wolffia globosa, an emerging functional food and potential future food source, is rich in phytochemicals associated with health-promoting properties. Harnessing W. globosa-derived nanovesicles (WGNVs) represents a promising strategy for expanding the biomedical applications of this plant. In this study, WGNVs were isolated and characterized, and their neuroprotective potential was evaluated in vitro. The isolated WGNVs exhibited nanoscale dimensions and a lipid bilayer structure. Biochemical analyses revealed substantial total phenolic and flavonoid contents, alongside intrinsic antioxidant activities. Untargeted metabolomic profiling identified a diverse repertoire of metabolites, including major constituents subsequently validated using independent analytical approaches. These findings provided a foundation for investigating the neuroprotective effects of WGNVs in a methylglyoxal (MGX)-induced model of neuronal oxidative stress. High-resolution confocal microscopy demonstrated the cellular localization of WGNVs within neuronal cells, providing evidence of interactions between plant-derived nanovesicles and neuronal cells. WGNV treatment attenuated MGX-induced free radical accumulation and oxidative stress responses while preserving cellular morphology integrity. Collectively, this study provides foundational evidence of the physicochemical characteristics, metabolite composition, and in vitro neuroprotective potential of WGNVs. These findings highlight WGNVs as a promising naturally derived nanocarrier platform for investigating plant-animal interkingdom interactions and exploring potential therapeutic applications across a broad range of biomedical fields.

title: Region-dependent regulation of Tau phosphorylation by Glycerophosphodiester Phosphodiesterase 2 in a mouse model of tauopathy
abstract: Hyperphosphorylation of Tau promotes its aggregation and neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) formation, contributing to neuronal dysfunction and neurodegeneration in diseases such as Alzheimer's Disease (AD) and AD-related dementias (ADRDs). However, the mechanisms underlying dysregulated Tau phosphorylation under pathological contexts remain unclear. Glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase 2 (GDE2) is a six-transmembrane enzyme that acts at the cell surface to cleave the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchor that tethers a subclass of proteins to the membrane. Here, we show that in the PS19 tauopathy mouse model, GDE2 disruption modulates Tau phosphorylation by transiently decreasing Tau's propensity for aggregation through region-specific regulation of local kinase environments. In the cortex, GDE2 ablation in 6-month-old PS19 male mice (PS19;Gde2KO) reduces Tau phosphorylation at Serine (S)202/Threonine (T)205, T212, and S396 but increases S262 phosphorylation in the hippocampus of 6-month-old PS19;Gde2KO male and female mice. Consistent with these changes, in males, Glycogen Synthase Kinase-3 / {beta} (GSK3 / {beta}) activity is decreased in the cortex, while AKT activity is increased in both males and females in the hippocampus, with no changes in protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) activity. Primary cortical neurons from PS19;Gde2KO animals showed reduced Tau phosphorylation at S202/T205, implying cell-autonomous roles for neuronal GDE2 in this process. GDE2 overexpression in heterologous SH-SY5Y cells increased Tau phosphorylation at S202/T205, while a catalytically inactive form of GDE2 did not, suggesting that GDE2 regulation of target GPI-anchored protein surface activity is required to modulate Tau phosphorylation. Taken together, our study identifies GDE2 as a component of the complex regulatory network that controls Tau phosphorylation in the context of tauopathy and provides insight into putative pathways relevant to Tau pathologies observed in disease.

title: Dissociable norepinephrine and dopamine representations during strategic decision-making and reward learning
authors: Aloor, J.; Sit, T. P.; Geuter, J.; Tutt, J. O.; Duan, C. A.
abstract: Adaptive decision-making in competitive environments requires learning from immediate reward outcomes while tracking longer-timescale information to adjust behavioural strategies and remain unpredictable against others. Dopamine (DA) and norepinephrine (NE) have long been implicated in reward-guided behaviours, but their contributions to strategic choice remain unclear. We trained mice to play a zero-sum matching pennies game against a computer opponent that exploited regularities in their choice and reward history, such that optimal performance required stochastic choice decoupled from immediate reward. We combined fibre photometry recordings, behavioural and neural modelling, and a within-subject multi-task design to determine how NE and DA contribute to strategic choice in the matching pennies game versus reward-guided behaviour in a two-armed bandit (2AB) task. DA responses were dominated by trial-by-trial reward outcomes and consistently tracked model-derived reward prediction errors (RPE) across tasks and behavioural states. In contrast, NE activity reflected salient task events, predicted upcoming choice switches, and tracked longer-timescale variables including model-inferred behavioural strategy and average reward rate. In addition, NE responses were selectively enhanced following rewarded switches when these outcomes were informative for deciding whether to stay in or switch from the current strategy; and this enhancement could not be explained by RPE. Incorporating pre-choice NE activity into a reinforcement-learning model to modulate choice generation improved model prediction in matching pennies but not in the 2AB task. Together, these findings reveal complementary neuromodulatory correlates of competitive decision-making across timescales: DA primarily guides learning from immediate outcomes through RPE, whereas NE additionally represents contextual information and choice stochasticity relevant for shaping long-term strategies.

title: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNS for Flexible Working Memory
authors: Lu, K.; Chu, T.; TUERHONG, A.; Sun, Y.; Luo, H.; Fang, F.; WU, S.
abstract: Oscillatory phase coding (OPC) is widely observed in neural systems and has been implicated in cognitive functions such as memory and sequence processing. However, its computational role and neural substrates remain largely unclear. Here, we studied OPC by training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, we found that OPC emerges in the RNN spontaneously: the memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm, with oscillation amplitude encoding item identity and phase encoding serial order. Ablation studies identified three key elements required for OPC: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis revealed the emergence of content and time cells in the trained RNN, and they process item identity and sequence order separately. Recurrent connectivity analysis revealed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups. Inspired by these findings, we proposed a neural circuit model which reproduces OPC through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. Together, this study reveals how OPC arises from network structures and task demands, offers insights into the implementation and computational mechanisms of OPC in biological systems, and inspires us to develop computational models for human-like cognitive functions.

title: Biomarkers indicate altered outer retinal fluid homeostasis in the absence of Kv2.1/Kv8.2 channels.
authors: Laird, J. G.; Soetedjo, J.; Inamdar, S. M.; Bock, A. R.; Ataman, E. S.; Pufall, M. A.; Berkowitz, B. A.; Baker, S. A.
abstract: Purpose: Photoreceptor Kv2.1/Kv8.2 voltage-gated potassium channels carry an outward potassium current, helping to set the resting membrane potential and to shape dim light responses. Because potassium flux in the outer retina influences extracellular osmolarity and fluid distribution, we hypothesized that Kv2.1/Kv8.2 channels also contribute to fluid homeostasis in this region of the retina. Methods: OCT imaging was performed in Kv8.2 heterozygous (Het) and knockout (KO) mice aged ~5 weeks under dark- and light-adapted conditions. Light-dark differences in the distance between the external limiting membrane (ELM) and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) ({Delta}ELM-RPE) were calculated to quantify light-evoked outer retinal expansion, a biomarker associated with changes in subretinal space (SRS) fluid handling. As a secondary outcome, outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness was also measured under both lighting conditions. Retinal gene expression was assessed by RNA-seq and droplet digital RT-PCR. Retinal protein expression was determined by western blotting and immunolabeling. Results: {Delta}ELM-RPE was significantly reduced in Kv8.2 KO mice compared with Het controls, indicating altered light-evoked outer retinal dynamics compatible with changes in subretinal space fluid handling. ONL thickness exhibited a small but significant light-dark change that was different between genotypes. Transcriptomic analyses revealed upregulation of osmosensitive genes, including osmolyte transporters and aquaporins. AQP1 protein expression in photoreceptors increased. Conclusions: These findings are consistent with altered outer retinal fluid homeostasis following loss of Kv8.2 and support a model in which photoreceptor potassium efflux contributes to osmotic water movement into the subretinal space.

title: Integrated metabolomics and proteomics from voxelated cortical hemispheres of adult rhesus monkeys
authors: Wu, Q.; Brigande, A. M.; Lutz, M. W.; Shi, P.; Disney, A.
abstract: The spatial organization of molecular networks across cortex likely contributes to differences in local circuit vulnerability in aging and Alzheimer's disease; yet many existing molecular datasets sacrifice spatial structure, sampling only a handful of regions per brain. Here, we present a framework for generating spatially registered, paired metabolomic and proteomic maps across an entire cortical hemisphere of an adult rhesus monkey, at millimeter resolution. One hemisphere each from two animals was harvested under controlled conditions, approximately flattened, and hand dissected at different sampling resolutions (roughly 2.5 and 4 mm/side) into tissue voxels. Each voxel was split after homogenization and extraction to provide matched aliquots for targeted metabolomics and deep untargeted proteomics. To handle these high dimensional data, we developed PChclust, a principal component guided feature clustering algorithm. For cross omic integration, we developed a spatially regularized sparse canonical correlation analysis (sr-sCCA), which incorporates spatial neighborhood structure via graph Laplacian smoothing. We recover meaningful biology: Molecular similarity between neighboring voxels decayed with distance in both modalities, confirming that voxelation captures spatially organized biological variance. The sr-sCCA identified joint proteome-metabolome components with coherent cortical gradients that were conserved across animals. Pathway enrichment analysis recovered brain relevant ontologies and reconstructed complete metabolic circuits from single voxels.

title: Multi-scale place fields provide a predictive basis for hierarchical control
authors: Yu, C.; Maimon, S. R.; Rich, P. D.; Eliav, T.; Las, L.; Lee, A. K.; Ulanovsky, N.; Lengyel, M.
abstract: Hippocampal place cells typically exhibit unimodal spatial selectivity in small enclosures, but express multiple, irregularly spaced fields in environments of naturalistic scale. However, existing predictive-map theories of the hippocampus do not scale well to large environments and do not account for these heterogeneous place field characteristics. Here, we introduce the factorised hierarchical successor representation (fHSR), a predictive map that supports hierarchical control using subgoal-directed subroutines. We show that the fHSR allows efficient generalisation across tasks, scaling favourably with environmental size, and it reproduces key statistical and topological characteristics of multi-scale CA1 place cell activity in rats and bats. Analyses of experimental data further confirmed a novel prediction of the fHSR: population firing rates exhibit spatial periodicity with a characteristic wavelength independent of environmental size. These results identify the integration of hierarchical control and predictive representations as a normative principle that unifies efficient navigation with the spatial organisation of hippocampal activity.

title: Active vision modulates early cortical stages of visual processing: Evidence from MEG and eye-tracking
authors: Huber-Huber, C.; De Lange, F. P.
abstract: Vision is fundamentally active. Humans and other mammals make several saccadic eye movements per second. This feature of mammalian vision has received increasing interest across the last decades and many behavioural and neurophysiological studies have investigated how the visual system accounts for the effects of self-generated motion (efference copy) in perceptual processing. Still, it is often believed that, besides accounting for the efference copy and for the rhythmic modulation of activity due to perpetual saccade-fixation cycles, active vision does not further modulate neural processing of visual input obtained during periods of fixation. In contrast, using a gaze-contingent trans-saccadic change design with concurrent MEG and eye-tracking data recording from human participants, we find sequential history effects in visual cortices. Harnessing the preview effect, we show that primary visual and ventral occipital cortices respond differently when eye-movements bring objects into focus compared to when the same objects appear during steady fixation. Specifically, we find that sequential modulations of cortical processing across saccades, in the form of preview effects, are increased during active vision compared to steady-gaze control conditions. Our data also show that these sequential modulations cannot be explained by any type of adaptation alone. Our study, therefore, provides an update on the role of active vision in modulating cortical function.
